Agone
uh-GON
adv. (archaic, = ago)
Archaic form of ago, from Old English agan (past participle of agan, to pass away), the older full form from which ago is a worn-down survival; appearing once in the Authorized Version.

Biblical Definition

My master left me, because three days agone I fell sick.

Agone appears once in the Authorized Version, in the mouth of an unnamed Egyptian servant found starving in the field, abandoned by his Amalekite master after falling ill. The word is simply the fuller, older form of ago, and the man uses it to answer David's question about how long he has gone without food or water: three days agone. The moment is small but consequential — this servant, cast off by his own master for the crime of sickness, becomes in the next verses the very man who guides David to the Amalekite raiding camp, enabling David to recover the wives, children, and goods of Ziklag that had been carried away. Agone marks the precise measure of his abandonment (three days) that in turn becomes the measure of David's mercy: David feeds him, revives him, and in exchange receives the intelligence that leads to total recovery of everything lost. The word itself is unremarkable, but the sentence it completes turns an act of cruelty (abandonment for sickness) into the hinge of a whole chapter's deliverance.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828), from AGONE: gone by; past; the fuller archaic form of ago, of which ago is a contraction.

AGONE, adv. Ago; past; gone by, as time.

AGONE is the older, fuller form; AGO is its worn-down survival in later English.

Both forms measure elapsed time from the moment of speaking.

AGONE appears once in the Authorized Version, in the speech of a rescued Egyptian servant.

In 1 Samuel 30:13 the word measures the three days since the servant was abandoned and fell sick.

Key Scripture

1Sa 30:13 — "And David said unto him, To whom belongest thou? and whence art thou? And he said, I am a young man of Egypt, servant to an Amalekite; and my master left me, because three days agone I fell sick."

Modern Corruption

There is no live postmodern redefinition of this ordinary archaic adverb; the entry exists to note that a single small word of measured time becomes, in its narrative context, the hinge of a whole chapter of deliverance.

expand to see more

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. Agone is simply the older form of ago, retaining the same sense across the centuries.

The principle to recover is not a corrected meaning but a right reading of what a small measured detail accomplishes in narrative: 'three days agone' fixes the exact span of the servant's abandonment, and that precise span becomes, within a few verses, the very information that lets David overtake the Amalekites and recover everything Ziklag had lost — an ordinary word of time-telling doing weighty narrative work.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Agone occurs once, in the mouth of the abandoned Egyptian servant whose rescue by David leads directly to the recovery of Ziklag's captives and goods.

expand to see more

Agone in 1 Samuel 30:13 measures the three days since the servant's master abandoned him.

The servant was left to die because he fell sick, a small cruelty within a larger raid.

David feeds and revives the servant before asking anything further of him.

The servant's knowledge of the Amalekite camp becomes the key to David's pursuit.

The chapter ends with David recovering all that was taken, losing nothing.

Usage

"Three days agone I fell sick — the exact measure of an abandonment about to be reversed."

"My master left me — cruelty answered, a few verses later, by David's mercy."

"The small detail of time becomes the key that unlocks the whole chapter's deliverance."
